assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene opened a new platform in which a single tuning knob produces flat bands, correlated insulators, superconductivity and later topological states. It is a clear case of quantum matter surprising theorists and experimenters alike, in the spirit of graphene itself. The Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum-model prediction of the magic angle, followed by the 2018 experiments, gives the theory-experiment tie I value.
assessment.attribution: The Bistritzer-MacDonald theory and the Jarillo-Herrero group experiments are the decisive pair. Three names fit the prize rule and give a clean theory-plus-experiment configuration. Earlier twisted-bilayer theory by others and the Cao et al. co-authors are not in the supplied credit, so some allocation questions remain.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed independently by many groups across transport, scanning probes and spectroscopy since 2018, and the field is large and still growing. The interpretation of the superconducting pairing is not settled, but the central discovery of correlated phases in flat bands is robust. Recognition would be timely.
uncertainties: Pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is unresolved.
Sample-to-sample variation in twist-angle disorder affects reproducibility of details.
Credit to other theorists of twisted bilayers and to experimental co-authors is not captured by the supplied names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect are a major conceptual shift in how band structure is classified, linking mathematics of topology to measurable edge transport. The prediction followed by the HgTe quantized edge conductance is exactly the kind of verified discovery with a clear physical core. Its impact spans materials theory, spectroscopy of surface states and spintronics.
assessment.attribution: Kane (with Mele) supplied the theory and Molenkamp the first experimental realization in HgTe quantum wells. The candidate bundles quantum anomalous Hall work through Xue, but a two-person prize on prediction and first realization is cleaner. Contributions by Mele, Bernevig, Zhang, Hasan and others (partly in neighbouring candidates) complicate a fair division.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed across many materials by ARPES, transport and scanning probes over nearly two decades. Quantum anomalous Hall realization is also reproduced. The core is mature, and recognition is arguably overdue, though the overlap with candidate B030 and the 2016 topological-phases prize requires care.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2016 prize on topological phases and with the separate Hasan and Mele candidacies.
Hard to separate theory credit among Kane, Mele, Bernevig, Zhang, Fu without a prize slot for each.
Whether the quantum anomalous Hall part should be handled separately.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamical mean-field theory is the first systematic non-perturbative tool for strongly correlated electrons and, combined with DFT, underlies realistic predictions for correlated materials. It explained the Mott transition and the coexistence of Hubbard bands with quasiparticle peaks. This is close to my own field, where reproducible computation tied to measured spectra matters, and its impact on materials theory is deep.
assessment.attribution: Metzner and Vollhardt introduced the infinite-dimension limit, and Georges and Kotliar established the mapping onto an impurity problem; Müller-Hartmann and others also contributed. The three supplied names form a defensible set, though the omission of Metzner and Müller-Hartmann is a real concern.
assessment.maturity: Mature: thirty years of use, validated against photoemission, optical and neutron data, and now implemented in many codes. Accuracy limits (spatial correlations, double counting in DFT+DMFT) are known and being addressed, but the framework is stable. Recognition is timely or somewhat late.
uncertainties: Theory-only discovery; a Nobel in physics usually favours a measured consequence, and the connection to specific experiments is by many groups rather than one decisive test.
Credit to Metzner and Müller-Hartmann.
Systematic uncertainties in DFT+DMFT applications.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Room-temperature tunnel magnetoresistance and giant TMR in MgO junctions made spin-dependent tunnelling a practical, large effect, underpinning magnetic read heads and MRAM. It also tested spin-filtering theory quantitatively, since coherent tunnelling through MgO was predicted by first-principles calculations before the experiments. That mix of verified physics and technology is attractive, though the 2007 prize on GMR already covers part of the field.
assessment.attribution: Moodera and Miyazaki reported room-temperature TMR in 1995 in amorphous alumina junctions; Parkin and Yuasa/Djayaprawira groups reported giant MgO TMR in 2004. Yuasa and Djayaprawira and the theorists Butler and Mathon are absent from the supplied credit, which weakens the configuration.
assessment.maturity: Very mature, with two decades of commercial use and many confirmations. Recognition is late rather than premature, and the risk is that the discovery is considered too incremental after Fert and Grunberg.
uncertainties: Incremental relative to the 2007 GMR prize.
Credit for MgO giant TMR is split among groups not on the list, including Yuasa and theorists Butler and Mathon.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Trapped-ion quantum computation and simulation turned the Cirac-Zoller proposal into gate operations, entangled states and programmable quantum simulators with record fidelities. It shows that quantum mechanics offers control of individual particles for technology, and it is a leading platform for quantum computing.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller proposed the ion-trap quantum computer in 1995; Blatt realized the gates, entanglement and large-scale algorithms. Wineland and Monroe, important to this field, are outside the supplied credit; Wineland already shared the 2012 prize for ion control.
assessment.maturity: Mature: independent groups worldwide have confirmed high-fidelity gates and entanglement, and commercial devices exist. Recognition is timely, but the 2012 prize and the circuit 2025 prize on quantum devices narrow the room.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 Wineland prize.
Exclusion of Monroe and Wineland, who are not among the supplied names.
Competition from other quantum-computing platforms for recognition.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical-lattice quantum simulation of Hubbard physics, from the Mott insulator transition to single-site imaging, gives experimental access to many-body models that I and other theorists can only approximate. It sets controlled benchmarks for correlated-electron theory.
assessment.attribution: Jaksch and Zoller proposed the Bose-Hubbard realization; Greiner, Bloch and Hänsch observed the superfluid-Mott transition; Bloch, Greiner and Esslinger drove fermionic and single-site work. Five credited names cannot all be honoured, and I chose theory plus the two most associated experiments.
assessment.maturity: Mature and confirmed independently in many laboratories, with continuing progress in quantum-gas microscopy. Recognition is timely, but its link to a single discovery is diffuse.
uncertainties: Diffuse discovery with many contributors, including Jaksch, Hänsch and others not credited.
Overlap with the 2001 BEC prize and the 2012 and 2022 quantum prizes.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks at 10^-18 precision realize magic-wavelength trapping and enable searches for variation of constants and relativistic geodesy. The proposal and its realization are clear, quantitative and confirmed.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice clock, and Ye's group brought it to record precision with strontium. Two laureates fit the evidence. Other clock groups (Ludlow, Hinkley, Schioppo, NIST ion clocks) are not credited.
assessment.maturity: Mature and independently reproduced at several national laboratories, though the redefinition of the second is still pending. Recognition is timely, with the 2005 frequency-comb prize as precedent.
uncertainties: Closeness to the 2005 prize for optical frequency combs.
Possible need to include other clock pioneers.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Altermagnetism is a newly classified collinear magnetic order, with compensated moments, spin-split bands and no net magnetization. It matters to my own field of magnetism and electronic structure, where DFT predicts spin splitting that spectroscopy has confirmed, and it may enable spintronics without stray fields.
assessment.attribution: Smejkal, Sinova and Jungwirth made the symmetry-based classification and predictions, with earlier contributions by others such as Hayami, Yuan and Zunger and the first spectroscopic confirmations by experimental groups not credited. The supplied trio is credible but the allocation is unsettled.
assessment.maturity: Young: ARPES and other evidence for MnTe and CrSb appeared in 2024, and the field is just maturing. Recognition now would be premature relative to the other candidates, though the concept is robust.
uncertainties: Only a few years of independent confirmation.
Priority conflicts with Hayami, Yuan, Zunger and others.
Experimental confirmation by groups not named in the credit.
